body.note: ICRP Publication 23 (1975) gives only an upper limit for a 70 kg reference adult: less than 0.048 g.

crystal.structure: rhombohedral (β-boron type: framework of B12 icosahedra)

temperature.note: The COD entry does not state the temperature of the measurement.

crystal.reference: Callmer, B. (1977). Acta Crystallographica, Section B 33, 1951.
crystal.note: β-rhombohedral boron is the thermodynamically stable form at ambient conditions; α-rhombohedral boron (COD 9017847) is metastable. Cell given on hexagonal axes. Two sites are partially occupied; the occupancy-weighted atom count per hexagonal cell is given in atoms_per_cell, and divided by 3 for the primitive rhombohedral cell (Pearson hR105; hR111 and hR141 also appear in the literature depending on how partial sites are counted). Temperature not stated in CIF.

production.basis: world production, all forms (boron minerals and compounds)

unitValue.note: Price, average unit value of combined imports, cost, insurance, and freight, dollars per metric ton [Boron], 2025; per kg of the material named, as USGS gives it.

critical.note: The 2023 study assessed 'boron/borate' (borate minerals); the Regulation lists 'boron'.

molarHeatCapacity.note: At 25 °C and 1 bar, per mole of atoms, for the form stable at 25 °C (CRC Handbook, 95th ed.).

uses.text: The glass and ceramics industries are the main users of borates, including specialty glasses.
Borates also go into insulation, abrasives, cleaning products and insecticides, and into making semiconductors.
Used in nuclear energy, and to harden steel and glass.

sectors.text: Boron goes into electrolysers that make hydrogen, wind turbines, solar panels and heat pumps, according to the JRC's study of strategic technologies.
Boron goes into fuel cells, electric traction motors and industrial heat pumps, according to the JRC's study of strategic technologies.
Boron goes into the networks that carry data, data centres (storage and servers) and phones, tablets and laptops, according to the JRC's study of strategic technologies.

allotropes.name: β-rhombohedral boron
allotropes.note: The stable form: a complicated framework of linked B₁₂ icosahedra, more than 100 atoms per cell.

allotropes.name: α-rhombohedral boron
allotropes.note: The simplest form: B₁₂ icosahedra packed in layers, 12 atoms per cell; red, transparent crystals.

allotropes.name: Amorphous boron
allotropes.note: A brown powder without long-range order.

hazards.note: Aggregated by PubChem from 485 reports by companies to the ECHA C&L Inventory; the percentage after a statement is the share of reports that give it. 52.2 % of the reports (253 of 485) say boron does not meet the GHS hazard criteria.

crust.note: Earth's crust, as given (mg/kg is parts per million by mass).

ocean.note: Sea water, mg/L read as mg/kg: a litre of sea water is taken as one kilogram (it is slightly heavier; the difference cannot be seen on a logarithmic scale).

body.note: ICRP Publication 23 (1975) gives only an upper limit for a 70 kg reference adult: less than 0.048 g.

origin.note: Paper Sect. 3.5: 'Be and B are supposed to be produced by cosmic rays [Prantzos et al. 1993], which is not included in our model either.' Empty box in Fig. 39. Value is the paper's qualitative statement, not a modelled fraction.

bonding.note: B₁₂ icosahedra linked into a hard three-dimensional network.

air.text: Crystalline boron is very inert at room temperature; impure or amorphous boron is more reactive.

water.text: Does not react with water at room temperature.

acids.text: Crystalline boron resists most acids; hot concentrated nitric acid oxidises it to boric acid.

splitting.note: Atomic-beam magnetic resonance (Lew and Title 1960), as tabulated in arXiv:1511.08928 Table V. Splitting derived as 2A. Another review attributes the same number to Harvey, Evans and Lew (1972).

plantRole.text: Taken up as boric acid; cross-links the pectin rhamnogalacturonan II in cell walls, so a shortage first harms growing tips, flowers and pollen tubes.

humanRole.text: May help bone and brain function, but no essential role in humans has been proven.

biology.note: Human: no EFSA dietary reference value.

roles.text: Not shown to be essential, but adding boron to low-boron feeds strengthened the bones of broiler chickens and laying hens in several trials.
Cyanobacteria need it to build working nitrogen-fixing heterocysts, and a signal molecule bacteria use to sense their own numbers contains borate.

deficiency.text: Growing points suffer first: the youngest leaves and buds are deformed or die, stems thicken or crack, and flowers and young fruit drop. Typical disorders are hollow stem in broccoli, heart rot in sugar beet, brown heart in swede and turnip, and internal cork in apples.

Grasses such as wheat need several times less boron than clover and most other broad-leaved plants, probably because their cell walls hold less pectin. Boron shortage is thought to be more widespread in crops worldwide than shortage of any other micronutrient.

toxicity.text: Too much boron is common in dry regions, on soils formed from marine sediments and where irrigation water is rich in boron; older leaves yellow and die back from their tips and edges. Tolerance ranges from about 100 mg per kg of leaf dry matter in maize to about 1,000 in squash.

soil.text: Boric acid washes out of soil easily, so shortage is common in rainy regions and the tropics, and on sandy, alkaline or heavily limed soils; dry topsoil also cuts the supply to roots.

partners.text: Legumes need four to five times more boron to build root nodules than to grow roots, so boron shortage means fewer and poorer nodules and less nitrogen fixed.

forest.text: In Scots pine stands in northern Sweden that were fertilised with nitrogen, boron shortage killed the leading shoots; side shoots took over and the stems grew crooked.

food.text: Seeds from boron-short plants can look normal yet give more weak or abnormal seedlings, as found in black gram.

levels.part: top third of the plant shortly before flowering
levels.note: Table 8.3, row citing Neubert et al. (1970): deficiency <20, sufficiency 31–80, toxicity >100.

levels.part: young mature leaves from the top of the plant
levels.note: Table 8.3, row citing Neubert et al. (1970): deficiency <10, sufficiency 30–75, toxicity >200.

levels.part: leaves from the base of new shoots

levels.note: Possible deficiency below this level (Carter 1992, cited in chapter 13); the book says micronutrient critical levels in trees are not well established.

environment.text: Plants need boron, yet in dry regions soils formed from marine sediments, or irrigation water rich in boron, give them too much: older leaves yellow and then die from their tips and margins.

history.nameOrigin: From borax, its best-known compound (a word traced to the Arabic buraq and Persian burah), given the ending of carbon.
history.note: Gay-Lussac and Thénard in Paris and Davy in London obtained it independently in 1808, all by heating boric acid with potassium.

prose.text: Boron is a hard metalloid that appears as black, glittering crystals or a brown powder; we meet it in borax, in heat-resistant borosilicate glassware and, invisibly, in crops and other flowering plants, which need traces of it to hold their cell walls together. About 19.65 % of natural boron is boron-10, a nucleus that captures slow neutrons so readily that it is used in reactor control rods and radiation shielding. The atom's ground configuration, [He] 2s² 2p¹, leaves a single unpaired p electron (ground term ²P°₁/₂), and boron-10 has an unusually large nuclear spin, 3, for so light a nucleus.
